archetype.name: Bubble Team (volume offense, leaky net)
archetype.definition: A Winnipeg side whose star-driven scoring and power play keep it in the wild-card mix, but whose shot suppression, penalty kill and goaltending sit in the bottom third, so its record swings with how hot the shooters run.

report.headline: Six straight wins paper over a team still bleeding shots and saves
report.take:
Two seasons ago this was the best team on the site: 116 points, the league's top defense, and goaltending worth 40.9 goals above expected. Last year it fell to 82 points and 25th. This year's Jets sit in between. They are 10-8-3, 20th on the site, sixth in a crowded Central and level on record with Utah, on a pace of 90 points. That is bubble territory, and the profile underneath says they belong there.

The season has come in two halves. October was a 4-10 month that included a nine-game losing streak. November is 6-1, and the Jets carry a six-game winning streak into the week, with 27 goals over the last five games, 5.4 a game. The engine is the top of the lineup. Kyle Connor has 17 goals on 89 shots and ranks 4th among 128 left wingers. Mark Scheifele has 26 points, and Cole Perfetti is 9th of 240 centers. A power play converting 24.2% (12th) adds to it. The Jets also put 28.8 shots a game on net, 8th in the league, so the offense is not a mirage. It produces volume.

What the streak hides is the other end. Winnipeg allows 32 shots a game, the most in the league and 4.9 above the league average. It holds 48.4% of the 5-on-5 expected goals and 48% of the attempts, both in the 20s. The goaltending that once covered for everything no longer does: a .881 save percentage (27th) and -2.6 GSAx (23rd). Their 5-on-5 PDO of 100.1 is ordinary, but the all-situations figure is 98.9, well under the league's 100.6, and a 72.1% penalty kill (24th) shows where the extra goals come from. Even the last ten games, the stretch that includes the streak, show 41 goals allowed and a -2 differential. Two of the six wins came in overtime.

Where this goes depends on whether the shot wall shrinks. A November scoring rate of 4.57 a game will not hold. When it cools, a team giving up this many shots with league-average-or-worse goaltending drifts back toward .500. Josh Morrissey has played only 7 of 21 games, and the blueline behind Neal Pionk and Dylan Samberg has struggled. Getting him in the lineup is the most direct route to fixing the volume against. Until that happens, expect a team that fights for a wild card rather than the 2024-25 version.

strengths.title: Star scoring at the top
strengths.body: Connor, Scheifele and Perfetti are all top-12 at their positions on the site, and Connor's 17 goals come on 89 shots, so the volume is real rather than a few lucky bounces. Connor's goal rate will cool, but a trio this productive keeps the floor of the offense around league average or better. The depth behind them (Lowry, Barron, Björck) adds little, so the scoring is concentrated.

strengths.title: Shot volume and a working power play
strengths.body: Winnipeg ranks 8th in shots on goal a game, and its power play sits two points above the league average. Neither leans on unusual shooting luck: the team's all-situations shooting percentage is actually 22nd. That makes the offense the most sustainable part of the profile.

concerns.title: Most shots against in the league
concerns.body: At 32 shots allowed a game, the Jets give up more than any team, with sub-50% shares of expected goals and attempts at 5-on-5. This is structural, not a cold patch. Their goaltenders face a heavy workload nightly, and the defense ranks 21st in goals against. Unless the blueline changes, expect it to persist.

concerns.title: Goaltending and kill no longer bail out
concerns.body: The elite seasons rested on 40-plus goals saved above expected. This year the tandem is below zero: Stuart Skinner's .880 over 15 starts is the main drag, and the penalty kill is 24th. With 5-on-5 PDO at 100.1 and all-situations PDO at 98.9, the leaks show up on the kill and in non-even-strength play more than at 5-on-5.

concerns.title: Thin blueline behind the top pair
concerns.body: Morrissey has played just 7 games. Haydn Fleury's 35.4% expected-goals share and -8 have soaked up minutes in his place, and Mario Ferraro's 45% is little better. Opposing defensemen produce well above their norms against Winnipeg (29th), a sign of a back end getting pinned. A healthy Morrissey would change this most.

trend.note: A nine-game skid sank October at 4-10, and November flipped to 6-1 with a six-game win streak. The underlying shot numbers barely moved, so the swing is mostly finishing and timing.

weekAhead.headline: Four home games, all against teams ranked above Winnipeg
weekAhead.body:
The streak gets a real test: Ottawa, the Islanders, Vegas and Utah all come to Winnipeg, and all four sit higher on the site. Home ice helps, but every opponent except the Islanders out-chances its opponents better than the Jets do. Vegas is the class of the week.

The matchups split along special teams. Ottawa's power play is the league's worst, a reprieve for a shaky kill. Vegas and Utah bring top-four power plays that could punish it. The Islanders are the inverse problem: elite goaltending and a strong kill that can stall a hot offense. Utah, level with Winnipeg on record, looks like the shootout of the week, given its 31st-ranked goaltending and porous kill.

keyMatchups.title: Jets kill vs Vegas and Utah power plays
keyMatchups.body: Vegas converts 28.8% and Utah 34.7%, both in the league's top four. Winnipeg's 72.1% kill is 24th. Two nights where the penalty count could decide the result.

keyMatchups.title: Hot offense meets Islanders goaltending
keyMatchups.body: The Islanders' goalies are 11.9 goals above expected, 3rd in the league, behind a kill ranked 4th. They hold forwards under their usual output (7th). The Jets' recent scoring rate is least likely to survive this game. The Islanders also shoot little, which eases Winnipeg's shots-against problem for a night.

keyMatchups.title: Connor against Ottawa and Utah
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa holds centers well (3rd) but lets wingers produce above their norms (22nd). That points the Jets' offense through Connor rather than the center-heavy middle. Utah's goalies sit at -11.7 GSAx with a 70.4% kill, a matchup Winnipeg's power play should exploit.

weekAhead.watch: Shots against: if the Jets keep winning while still allowing 30-plus a night to these better teams, the streak is finishing, not improvement.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should stay around league average or a bit better, because it rests on shot volume and three top-end forwards rather than shooting luck. The November scoring burst, the 27 goals in five games and the overtime wins will fade. Pts vs Goal Diff already has them slightly ahead of their differential. The defensive profile is the binding constraint: the league's heaviest shot load and below-average goaltending make a goals-against rate in the low-to-mid 3s the likely norm.

That adds up to a team near its 90-point pace, somewhere in an 84-94 point range and roughly 37-43 wins. That is wild-card bubble in a deep Central. The upside case needs a healthy Morrissey trimming the shots against and Skinner climbing toward a .895 save percentage. The downside is the October version returning once the shooting cools.

confidence.note: 21 games with wild swings in results, but the shot and goaltending numbers have been steady.
